title: Do Digital Government and Fiscal Data Capacity Improve Budgetary Outcomes? Panel Evidence from the European Union
content: Governments hold more fiscal data than ever, and the reformed EU fiscal framework relies on timely monitoring, yet whether data capacity goes together with better budgetary outcomes remains untested across countries. We define data-driven fiscal governance as the capacity to produce, use and open fiscal data, and approximate it for the EU-27 with public indicators of digital government, fiscal data reliability and open data maturity. These measures are matched with real-time deficit projections and targets from the 2016–2024 Stability and Convergence Programmes and their first-release outturns, and analysed with two-way fixed effects and wild cluster bootstrap inference. Data capacity is not associated with more accurate current-year forecasts, although gains of around 0.2 percentage points of GDP remain possible and potentially meaningful. Higher digital government maturity goes together with larger deviations from one-year-ahead targets in both directions, but the association is fragile: it is not significant with a two-year lag, an alternative digital government measure or country-specific trends, and its weakening under strong medium-term frameworks does not survive a multiple-testing correction. The index components are weakly related, and fiscal data reliability is unrelated to all outcomes. General digital maturity appears to be a poor proxy for the fiscal use of data.
